title: Recording Baby Dodds on drums
summary: Russell's twelve hours of Baby Dodds talking about drums, the booklet, and the idea of one expert per instrument.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: So I sometimes get discouraged and wonder whether it's worth fooling with trying to preserve it. One thing, project I've worked on started, though, uh, around 1950, you might say, after the Jelly Roll tapes became known, I decided to record Baby Dodds talking about drums, and, uh, I got a little, uh, book that you might say was going to publish at that time, years ago. I recorded him maybe about 12 hours talking about drums. He'd already had a couple of strokes and wasn't too effective in playing, but he could still demonstrate his different instruments and some of the points he would talk about.

But, uh, it was, uh, the main idea was, uh, recorded it, but the main idea was to, uh, transcribe the talking and make a little booklet out of it with quite a few illustrations. It wasn't, uh, any, in any sense a drum method or anything, but he did, uh, talk about the, how the drums should fit into the New Orleans band and the right style to play. Mm-hmm. And he described his instruments and his own training and how he learned and, uh, a little bit about his life and, uh, a few little, colorful. He was a very good talker, anyway. So, it was a very interesting book. In fact, a lot of people have read it. And some people, I think, Bob Green, when he read it, said it's the best thing he ever read on, uh, New Orleans jazz to explain what it is. And somebody else said that maybe he'd talk like a poet. I mean, he's such a wonderful talker. Well, he did have that rhythmic sense as he said everything he did. He would sleep drums. He would think drums. He would eat drums. Every time when he's eating or sleeping, he'd be dreaming about drums. That's all he thought about. And, uh, to him, it was a regular musical instrument. Anyway, he gets into that for about 70 pages, that thing ran. So, um, the woman in Chicago, uh, uh, Mrs. Taggy, who, uh, helped transcribe the, uh, in fact, she did most of the transcribing of the baby Dodds talking and, and helped, uh, arranged the little booklet which we had baby to go through and approve before we finished it. So, uh, she said, why not use this as just one chapter in a book and get the different experts on each instrument? Uh, she said, like, uh, baby talks about the wonderful rhythm section he had on the boat there. He worked with, uh, Johnny St. Cyr and Pops Foster. And got somebody on each instrument to talk about instruments. And this was to give advice to young players. So they could, not necessarily could start from scratch and learn it, but if they were already interested, they could learn more about how their instruments should fit in. And a few other practical points sometimes, like, uh, say when I talked to Simeon and I decided to have him talk about clarinet. Even what kind of reads he likes and the advantages of the Albert over the BAME system, things of that kind.
